responses.strategic_rationale: This 3-year parasomnia research unit faces three fundamental tensions: (1) capturing rare, naturalistic nocturnal events versus the clinical artificiality of laboratory monitoring, (2) scaling staffing and data throughput to maximize participant enrollment while maintaining safety and annotation quality, and (3) justifying extended residential stays and operational overhead when single-night polysomnography is the diagnostic standard of care. The following levers address these core conflicts by forcing explicit trade-offs between fidelity and efficiency, between domestic authenticity and measurement precision, and between participant retention and data yield.

levers.name: Stay Duration Architecture
levers.consequences: Lengthening individual participant stays (up to 10 weeks) increases event capture probability and longitudinal within-person pattern characterization, but creates booking bottlenecks that reduce total participant throughput and forces extended commitment-to-screening ratios that may suppress recruitment from those with limited leave availability. Conversely, capping stays at 2–3 weeks maximizes annual enrollment but risks substantial zero-event admissions, wasting facility capacity and staff time on unproductive residents.
options: Implement a staggered follow-up model where participants complete a 3-week baseline admission, return home for 4–6 weeks, and then participate in a second 2-week visit focused on targeted nights if their baseline capture rate fell below protocol thresholds, distributing the residential burden across two shorter episodes rather than one long stay.

Adopt a rolling 2-week fixed stay for all participants with no extension option, accepting higher rates of zero-event admissions in exchange for maximized annual throughput and predictable facility turnover, then post-hoc stratify results by whether events were captured versus not.

Establish a two-tier enrollment pathway: fast-track high-frequency parasomnia participants (self-reported 4+ episodes per month) into standard 3-week stays, and offer a separate 6–8 week extended-stay track for lower-frequency cases, explicitly accepting that the extended cohort will enroll more slowly but generate richer within-person phenotyping data for a subset.
levers.review_lever: Longer stays reduce recruitment flexibility and burden families, while shorter stays risk wasting facility utilization on non-productive admissions; the three options do not address the clinical-vs-research tension of whether 10-week stays remain ethically proportionate to the parasomnia event frequency baseline used for inclusion.

levers.name: Technician Annotation Authority
levers.consequences: Granting night technicians real-time decision authority over which nights receive escalated full-PSG montage (based on flagged suspicious events) accelerates responsive event capture and reduces false-negative misses, but introduces inter-technician variability in flagging sensitivity and specificity, potentially creating systematic bias in which events enter the dataset. Conversely, pre-scheduling all enhanced nights (night 1, mid-stay, final night) eliminates technician bias but sacrifices responsive escalation and may miss recurrence opportunities that cluster outside those fixed windows.
options: Empower night technicians to escalate to full PSG within 2 hours of flagging a suspected parasomnia event during low-burden monitoring nights, using a simple decision tree (movement amplitude exceeding threshold AND vocalization present OR bed exit attempted), with weekly review audits and monthly retraining to track technician drift.

Pre-schedule all enhanced-PSG nights as fixed calendar dates (arrival night, nights 7–8 mid-stay, final night) for every participant, supplemented by an optional technician-triggered escalation protocol only if three suspicious events are flagged within a single 24-hour window, constraining technician discretion.

Implement a hybrid model where technicians flag suspicious events in real time but must obtain same-night or next-morning approval from the on-call senior researcher (PI or postdoctoral researcher) before escalating to full PSG, adding a gate that prevents novice technician over-escalation while preserving responsiveness and limiting overnight bottlenecks.
levers.review_lever: Technician discretion increases event capture but introduces bias; pre-scheduling ensures consistency but sacrifices responsiveness; none of the options explicitly addresses how technician fatigue or participant-technician familiarity drift might influence flagging behavior over a 10-week admission.

levers.name: Sensor Tier Harmonization
levers.consequences: The three-tier sensor model (low-burden, enhanced-PSG, escalation) generates vast heterogeneous data streams that require asynchronous alignment and motion-artifact filtering tailored to each tier's sensor suite, slowing post-hoc curation and complicating event-triage model training on mixed-quality input. Standardizing to a single high-resolution sensor suite every night eliminates alignment overhead and improves algorithm robustness, but triples electricity costs, generates overwhelming raw data volume, occupies technician time with streaming monitoring of 8 suites simultaneously, and risks participant discomfort from excessive electrode density that suppresses naturalistic behavior.
options: Maintain the tiered model but impose strict BIDS-compatible data structure requirements at acquisition time, including automated clock synchronization via NTP, parallel motion-artifact flags from each sensor tier, and segregated annotation workflows that train the event-triage algorithm on enhanced-PSG nights only, treating low-burden nights as validation-only.

Switch to full-resolution PSG montage every night for all participants, accepting the operational burden of real-time technician monitoring and the participant discomfort trade-off, but purchasing commercial software that auto-scores standard EEG features (sleep stage, arousal count) in real time, reducing post-hoc annotation bottleneck.

Deploy a hybrid where nights 1–3 and final night use full PSG, and intervening nights use low-burden sensors plus triggered escalation, but introduce a mid-stay recalibration where participants rate comfort and sleep quality every 3 days and the clinical team may reduce electrode density for high-discomfort cases, preserving the tiered approach while flagging where the protocol might suppress naturalistic behavior.
levers.review_lever: The tiered model reduces participant burden but complicates data curation; full resolution every night solves curation but adds operational overhead and discomfort that may suppress the very behaviors the study aims to capture, and none of the options addresses how electrode density correlates with parasomnia event likelihood.

levers.name: Control Cohort Recruitment Timing
levers.consequences: Recruiting matched controls concurrently with parasomnia participants ensures contemporaneous sensor calibration and staffing efficiency but delays publication of participant-only phenotyping findings and requires pre-committing resources to two recruitment channels simultaneously, splitting technician and coordinator effort. Recruiting controls after the parasomnia cohort is enrolled reduces initial recruitment pressure and allows the team to optimize protocols based on early participant experience, but creates a temporal gap that introduces sensor drift, protocol modifications, and staffing turnover that makes meaningful matching less tenable and delays comparative benchmarking of the event-triage algorithm.
options: Enroll matched controls concurrently, targeting 1 control admission for every 1.5 parasomnia participants, with control recruitment routed through the same primary-care and neurologist networks using identical screening procedures but an exclusion criterion of any self-reported nocturnal movement or awakening, ensuring tight temporal matching and uniform sensor configuration.

Delay control enrollment until parasomnia recruitment reaches 35 participants at approximately month 18, then conduct controls over months 18–30 using identical protocols and sensor suites as they exist at that timepoint, accepting a 6-month offset in exchange for operational simplicity and allowing early publications on parasomnia phenotyping alone.

Implement a rolling control cohort where control admissions occur in alternating months with parasomnia admissions (e.g., months 1–2 parasomnia, month 3 control, months 4–5 parasomnia, month 6 control), balancing temporal matching against recruitment cadence and enabling algorithm benchmarking as data accumulates rather than all at study endpoint.
levers.review_lever: Concurrent controls ensure matching fidelity but dilute early recruitment effort; delayed controls simplify operations but weaken temporal alignment and defer algorithm benchmarking; none directly addresses whether the control population's absence of any nocturnal movement is itself clinically unrealistic or creates a non-comparable reference baseline.

levers.name: Inter-Rater Scoring Workflow
levers.consequences: Requiring two independent raters to score all captured events (per AASM criteria) establishes ground truth reliability but demands substantial time commitment from sleep medicine experts, creating a bottleneck where scoring lags data acquisition and limits the number of events the team can process within budget. Implementing single-rater scoring with algorithmic pre-triage reduces expert time but sacrifices reliability transparency and introduces single-scorer bias that the event-triage algorithm will learn to replicate. A hybrid approach (single rater for low-confidence events flagged by the algorithm, dual raters only for borderline or discordant cases) balances efficiency and quality but risks systematic undercounting of algorithm-excluded events.
options: Maintain dual-rater scoring for all captured events, with disagreement arbitration via consensus meeting chaired by the PI, and explicitly budget 0.5 FTE sleep medicine specialist time for year 2–3, accepting that scoring will lag data acquisition by 2–4 weeks and may constrain the final event count relative to raw captures.

Deploy a single-rater scoring model where the lead postdoctoral researcher or sleep medicine specialist scores all enhanced-PSG nights and escalation events, with a sub-sample of 20% of scored nights re-scored independently by a second rater to estimate inter-rater reliability retrospectively and report the uncertainty bound in publications.

Implement a three-tier scoring cascade: the algorithm provides confidence scores for suspected parasomnia events; high-confidence events (top 10% of algorithm output) undergo single-rater scoring; medium-confidence events undergo dual-rater scoring with consensus arbitration; low-confidence events are flagged for discussion but may be excluded from primary analysis if both raters assign low clinical probability.
levers.review_lever: Dual-rater scoring guarantees reliability but creates a labor bottleneck; single-rater reduces burden but sacrifices objectivity; three-tier triage may bias the final event sample toward high-confidence cases that are less representative of the full parasomnia spectrum.

levers.name: Facility Expansion Trigger Logic
levers.consequences: The plan defers expansion to 12 suites until pilot data demonstrate acceptable quality and safety; this staged approach controls financial risk and allows protocol refinement on a smaller footprint, but foregoes economies of scale in staff deployment, facility overhead, and sensor procurement spread over 8 versus 12 units. Conversely, committing to full 12-suite build-out at launch maximizes long-term cost efficiency and demonstrates early ambition to funders and recruiting clinicians, but locks substantial capital into infrastructure before validating demand, data quality, and the unit's ability to safely manage higher patient density and staffing complexity.
options: Remain at 8 suites throughout the 3-year period with no expansion, focusing resources on protocol validation and publication output, then propose a follow-up phase-two grant for expansion and intervention studies based on the de-identified dataset and proof-of-concept results, positioning the original unit as a methodologically validated pilot.

Build out the full 12 suites during year-one renovation but operate them in phased activation: suites 1–8 launch in month 3, suites 9–10 activate in month 12 after pilot data review, and suites 11–12 activate in month 18 only if enrollment and event-capture rates exceed thresholds, using contingent capital deployment to control risk while preserving expansion flexibility.

Execute a mid-study expansion decision point at month 18 where enrollment, safety, and staffing data determine whether to build out the remaining 4 suites; if thresholds are met (25+ enrolled, zero serious adverse events, technician retention >80%), renovation and equipping occurs in months 18–20 with expanded operations in months 21–36, accepting the risk that late expansion compresses the operational window.
levers.review_lever: Staged expansion reduces upfront capital risk but forgoes efficiency gains; full build-out maximizes long-term cost per participant but risks underutilization; none of the options explicitly addresses whether facility reputation and clinician referral patterns depend on visible capacity or enrollment velocity.

levers.name: Pharmaceutical Partnership Governance
levers.consequences: Forgoing industry partnership retains full operational independence and publication autonomy but eliminates potential supplemental funding and industry-driven early validation interest, forcing reliance on academic grants and placing the unit at risk if DFG renewal is delayed or unsuccessful. A formal partnership providing upside funding accelerates resource availability and creates externally-validated endpoints, but introduces competing priorities around proprietary data, reporting timelines, and scope creep toward drug-responsive phenotypes that may distract from the primary methods-validation and longitudinal characterization aims.
options: Maintain the planned independent academic structure with no pharmaceutical partnership, reserving partnership discussions for a phase-two proposal only after the core phenotyping dataset is complete and de-identified publications establish methodological credibility, signaling to potential partners that collaboration occurs from a position of proven capability.

Engage a pharmaceutical partner as a non-voting scientific collaborator with a formal data-use agreement: the partner receives quarterly updates, a 30-day pre-publication comment window, and access to de-identified datasets after study completion, but contributes supplemental funding (e.g., €400K) that covers enhanced escalation-night capacity without dictating analysis strategy.

Establish a limited-scope partnership where the industry partner funds a single sub-study within the protocol (e.g., dedicated neuropsychological phenotyping in REM sleep behavior disorder participants) rather than whole-unit support, maintaining operational independence for the core NREM parasomnia aims while generating co-authored publications on the partner-funded sub-aim.
levers.review_lever: Independence sacrifices resource upside; full partnership risks mission creep; the three options do not clarify under what conditions academic publication velocity or clinical relevance thresholds would trigger proactive partnership outreach.

responses.strategic_rationale: The Bonn parasomnia unit navigates three fundamental tensions: (1) naturalistic behavior capture versus clinical safety—the domestic setting suppresses artifacts but complicates event response; (2) dense physiological monitoring versus annotation sustainability—comprehensive data streams demand human scoring bottlenecks that scale poorly; (3) recruitment yield versus participant burden—longer stays increase event capture probability but risk dropouts and facility utilization gaps. The seven levers below address these core conflicts by determining how strictly to enforce safety trade-offs, how to distribute annotation labor across human and algorithmic pathways, how recruitment criteria balance event yield against screening overhead, how to phase capital expansion relative to operational proof-of-concept, how to position the matched control arm relative to case enrollment, how to structure the external advisory board's authority over resource reallocation, and how to sequence data-sharing governance relative to publication timelines.

levers.name: Safety Envelope versus Behavioral Authenticity
levers.consequences: Stricter safety protocols (e.g., continuous staff presence, wrist actigraphy during sleep, restricted window hardware) reduce injury risk but create a more clinical atmosphere that suppresses naturalistic parasomnia expression, potentially lowering event-capture rates. Conversely, relaxed safety boundaries preserve ecological validity but increase staffing complexity and liability exposure during nocturnal episodes.
options: Enforce continuous staff presence in the residential unit during all sleep hours, with a dedicated safety monitor stationed in a central observation room equipped with live audio and motion alerts from all suites.

Implement a hybrid model: unrestricted movement with passive environmental sensors (door alarms, bed pressure pads, infrared motion detection) triggering automated staff alerts only when thresholds suggest injury risk or egress patterns.

Adopt a risk-stratified approach where participants with documented prior injuries or high-frequency episodes receive continuous presence while lower-risk individuals operate under passive monitoring, reducing fixed staffing burden.
levers.review_lever: Continuous presence guarantees rapid response but may inflate clinical atmosphere and suppress naturalistic behavior; relaxed monitoring captures authentic events but concentrates staffing demands unpredictably. The three options do not address whether passive-sensor false-alarm rates will overwhelm staff response capacity during multi-suite events.

levers.name: Annotation Workflow Parallelization
levers.consequences: Current protocol requires two independent raters to score all nights post-hoc against AASM criteria, creating a sequential bottleneck—if average stay is 4 weeks at 8 active suites, that is roughly 2,240 nights per year requiring dual scoring. Introducing real-time technician flagging reduces post-hoc review scope but risks inconsistent criteria application and potential bias. Conversely, strict post-hoc dual-rater-only scoring ensures rigor but may delay publication timelines and require hiring additional scoring personnel.
options: Establish a quality-assurance tier where the night technician applies a simplified event-triage checklist in real time (movement + arousal + duration thresholds) and flags only high-confidence candidate episodes for subsequent dual-rater scoring, reducing post-hoc review by approximately 40 percent.

Hire a dedicated full-time scoring coordinator who applies a preliminary AASM-aligned classification immediately after each night, then both raters review only coordinator-flagged events and a random 20 percent of negative nights to check false-negatives, creating a three-stage funnel.

Maintain strict post-hoc dual-rater review of all nights without technician input, ensuring methodological purity but requiring contracted external scorers to absorb the 2,000-plus annual night load without delaying analysis.
levers.review_lever: Introducing technician flagging accelerates throughput but risks criterion drift and inter-rater disagreement on what constitutes a true parasomnia versus normal nocturnal movement. None of the options directly address how to validate that post-hoc scorers agree on technician-selected events versus rejected ones.

levers.name: Inclusion Threshold and Event-Yield Risk
levers.consequences: The current inclusion criterion (≥2 self-reported episodes per month) balances recruitment feasibility against event-capture probability, but recall bias and seasonal clustering mean some enrolled participants may generate zero captured events. Tightening inclusion criteria (e.g., ≥4 episodes/month or recent polysomnographic documentation of multiple events) increases per-participant yield but shrinks the eligible population and extends recruitment timelines. Loosening criteria (e.g., single prior episode confirmed by witness) expands the pool but dilutes event-capture rates and inflates the 20 percent unproductive-admission ceiling.
options: Adopt a two-tier enrollment pathway: prioritize participants with ≥4 self-reported episodes per month and at least one prior polysomnographic capture, while accepting participants with 2–3 episodes per month only after the pilot cohort (n=15–20) demonstrates acceptable event-yield rates, deferring recruitment burden.

Require all screened participants to complete a 2-week outpatient actigraphy-plus-sleep-diary run before residential admission to generate objective movement data that predicts residential capture yield, using actigraphy episode frequency as a continuous covariate in enrollment decisions.

Accept all screened participants meeting the 2-episodes-per-month criterion without actigraphy prequalification, but implement a staged stay protocol where participants with zero events in the first 2 weeks are offered discharge and rescheduling 3 months later if they wish, rather than extension to 10 weeks.
levers.review_lever: Stricter inclusion reduces recruitment pool size and delays startup; looser inclusion inflates non-productive admissions and facility occupancy volatility. The options do not resolve whether to accept borderline-inclusion participants (e.g., single-episode polysomnographic captures) when recruitment falls behind schedule.

levers.name: Capital Expansion Trigger and Facility Saturation
levers.consequences: Deferring expansion to 12 suites until month 24 (per plan) minimizes financial risk if pilot data quality proves poor, but if operational validation succeeds early (by month 12), the unit reaches 8-suite saturation and begins turning away eligible participants. Expanding to 12 suites by month 15 accelerates participant throughput and captures more events, but commits capital before full operational proof and may create idle suites if staffing or recruitment falters. Conversely, committing to 12-suite build-out from the start reduces phased costs but locks in upfront capital and facility overhead.
options: Delay 12-suite expansion until month 24 while piloting a temporary overflow protocol: when 8 suites are full, enroll participants into a sister facility at University Hospital Bonn's clinical sleep lab on a time-shared basis (same protocols, staff, scoring pipeline), de-risking capacity bottlenecks without permanent footprint expansion.

Trigger expansion to 10 suites (rather than 12) at month 15 if: enrollment rate ≥4 participants per month and event-capture rate ≥90 percent of plan assumptions, phasing the infrastructure and hiring incrementally to match observed demand.

Commit to full 12-suite renovation and staffing by month 12, accepting upfront financial risk in exchange for eliminating capacity constraints and demonstrating scale to DFG funders before the year-two operational phase.
levers.review_lever: Early expansion captures more data and demonstrates scale but risks underutilization if recruitment or event-yield falters; delayed expansion protects capital but may saturate the unit and create a bottleneck. None of the options address what to do if operational costs per participant prove higher than budgeted, reducing the marginal return of extra suites.

levers.name: Matched Control Enrollment Synchrony
levers.consequences: Enrolling matched controls concurrently with case participants (as assumed in current planning) ensures temporal alignment for sensor-algorithm benchmarking but increases per-night costs and staffing overhead proportionally—if cases occupy 4 suites and controls occupy 2 suites simultaneously, facility utilization is higher but fixed costs per case-event increase. Deferring control enrollment until after case phenotyping is complete reduces near-term staffing load and allows focusing recruitment on high-yield cases first, but delays the event-triage algorithm training and introduces temporal differences (e.g., seasonal sensor drift, software versioning) that complicate comparison.
options: Maintain parallel enrollment of cases and matched controls from month 6 onward, aiming for a 4:1 case-to-control ratio (40 cases, 10 controls) to balance benchmarking requirements against facility efficiency, accepting elevated overnight staffing costs for two additional suites.

Enroll all 50–70 case participants in the first 18 months, then dedicate months 19–30 to recruiting and retaining 15–20 matched controls under identical protocols, allowing control-group analysis to serve as a validation cohort for algorithm development without competing for recruitment resources.

Use a rolling cohort model: recruit controls in matched pairs immediately after every fifth case admission, distributing control enrollment evenly across the 3-year period and allowing incremental algorithmic validation as the case phenotyping dataset matures.
levers.review_lever: Concurrent controls maximize internal validity but inflate operational complexity; sequential controls reduce near-term burden but risk temporal confounds and delay algorithm benchmarking by 18 months. The options do not specify how to handle unmatched controls if case recruitment falls short of the 50–70 target.

levers.name: External Advisory Board Authority and Budget Gates
levers.consequences: Granting the scientific advisory board approval rights for budget reallocations above €50K (per plan) provides fiscal oversight and expert scrutiny but may slow operational decisions during urgent needs (e.g., emergency equipment repair, rapid staff hiring to cover absences). Conversely, concentrating reallocation authority entirely in the PI accelerates responsive decisions but increases risk of off-plan spending and reduces external accountability. A middle ground—allowing the PI to approve reallocations up to a threshold and requiring board sign-off for larger moves—balances agility and governance.
options: Establish a tiered approval matrix: PI authority for reallocations ≤€30K with board post-hoc review at quarterly meetings; €30–75K reallocations require asynchronous board consultation within 2 weeks; reallocations >€75K require board convening within 14 days, with emergency exceptions (safety incidents, compliance violations) allowing PI discretion if board is notified within 48 hours.

Maintain strict €50K threshold with mandatory board approval, but implement a 'presumptive approval' rule where if the board does not object in writing within 10 business days of a reallocation request, the PI proceeds automatically, reducing decision latency for non-controversial moves.

Reduce board oversight to strategic milestones (Aim-completion approval, publication sign-off, year-two funding allocation) while delegating all quarterly operational budget reallocations to the PI and study coordinator, requiring only annual reconciliation reports to the board.
levers.review_lever: Strict board gatekeeping ensures accountability but may paralyze operational agility; PI autonomy risks fiscal drift and reduces external oversight. The options do not address how to resolve conflicts if the board and PI disagree on a reallocation's scientific merit versus cost necessity.

levers.name: Data-Sharing Timeline and Publication Sequencing
levers.consequences: Publishing phenotyping and methods results before depositing the de-identified physiological dataset in a public repository (a typical 12–18 month lag) maximizes competitive advantage and allows the core team to produce secondary analyses first. However, it delays community access to the resource and risks external researchers conducting analyses in parallel. Accelerating data release (e.g., concurrent with first publication or within 6 months of close-out) fosters open science and enables rapid community validation but surrenders first-mover advantage on clinical insights and algorithmic applications.
options: Deposit de-identified physiological and sensor data in a recognized public repository (e.g., OpenNeuro) within 6 months of study close-out (month 36), contingent on publication of at least one major phenotyping manuscript, allowing the core team priority time for primary analyses while committing to timely release.

Release data immediately upon publication of the primary results manuscript (Aim 2 characterization), without awaiting completion of the event-triage algorithm, permitting external researchers to develop competing or complementary segmentation tools while core-team algorithm development continues in parallel.

Establish a managed-access data-sharing model: deposit data in a controlled repository with access granted only to researchers whose analysis plans are pre-approved by the advisory board and PI, maintaining quality control and preventing redundant or low-rigor secondary analyses.
levers.review_lever: Early release accelerates community science but cedes competitive advantage and publication priority; delayed release protects IP but risks obsolescence and external pressure. The options do not directly address whether de-identified video data (if later released) would require additional governance or whether commercial reuse of physiological data should be permitted.

responses.strategic_rationale: This parasomnia research unit must navigate three core tensions: (1) capturing infrequent, naturalistic behaviors without instrumenting the environment so heavily that it suppresses them; (2) balancing the longitudinal depth needed for phenotyping against finite facility capacity and budget constraints; (3) staffing 24/7 night operations safely while maintaining annotation quality and managing false-alarm burden as sensor volumes scale. The levers below target these trade-offs directly—positioning decisions around environmental design, sensor escalation logic, workforce composition, data-quality gatekeeping, and publication strategy that determine whether the unit becomes a sustainable research engine or a resource sink producing noise rather than signal.

levers.name: Naturalism Calibration and Detection Trade-off
levers.consequences: Choosing how visible and intrusive the monitoring ecosystem is fundamentally affects whether participants exhibit authentic parasomnias or suppress behaviors under observation. Highly visible cameras, prominent electrode setups, and obvious safety modifications reduce ecological validity but improve event capture certainty; conversely, minimizing environmental cues and relegating sensors to dry electrodes and ambient arrays preserves behavior fidelity but increases false-positive burden on annotation and triage algorithms. This balance directly shapes the utility of captured events for phenotyping and the credibility of absence-of-events claims in control participants.
options: Deploy cameras in corners with warm ambient lighting and introduce them during a one-week acclimatization period before formal monitoring, treating the environment as a familiar bedroom rather than a clinical lab space.

Equip suites with clinical-grade visible electrode montages and safety railings throughout, accepting a higher proportion of suppressed events in exchange for unambiguous physiological signal quality and uncontested safety documentation.

Rely primarily on hidden mattress and bed-frame sensors with minimal visible apparatus, using infrared cameras only when technician-flagged events occur, preserving naturalism at the cost of delayed full-resolution capture on first occurrence.
levers.review_lever: Invisible sensor arrays preserve behavior authenticity but shift the annotation bottleneck to real-time technician judgment about which partial-signal events warrant escalation; no option resolves the fundamental tension between ecological validity and detection completeness during the baseline-monitoring nights.

levers.name: Roster Flexibility and Night-Shift Continuity
levers.consequences: Staffing night coverage with a fixed 3-technician rotating roster ensures predictable labor costs and team cohesion but locks the unit into a staffing model sized to 8 active suites with minimal slack for illness, vacation, or unexpected surge in event-flagging workload. Alternatively, building a larger flexible pool with on-call backup increases payroll and coordination overhead but absorbs staffing shocks and allows expansion trials without rehiring. The choice cascades into whether the unit can safely and ethically extend stays for zero-yield participants or must discharge them promptly to preserve technician capacity.
options: Maintain a dedicated 3-person night team on rotating 12-hour shifts with strict leave-replacement budgeting, accepting a hard operational ceiling of 7 concurrent participants before staffing becomes unsafe.

Recruit a 4- to 5-person core team plus 1–2 part-time per-diem technicians on-call, absorbing higher baseline payroll to enable flexible capacity scaling and event-driven escalation nights without burnout risk.

Cross-train the day-shift clinical psychologist and data engineer as backup technicians for light-monitoring nights, minimizing new hires and reserving the core night team for high-event-yield periods and complex annotation decisions.
levers.review_lever: Flexible rosters address staffing volatility but blur role clarity and introduce training variance if part-time staff rotate infrequently; none of the three options structurally solve the annotation bottleneck if event frequency exceeds technician throughput.

levers.name: Escalation Night Trigger and Triage Burden
levers.consequences: Defining the threshold at which a technician-flagged partial-signal event prompts deployment of full PSG montage on an escalation night determines both the sensitivity of the capture model and the operational cost per event. Aggressive escalation (low threshold, many escalation nights per participant) guarantees clinical-grade recapture but taxes equipment, staffing, and the budget; conservative escalation (high threshold, fewer escalation nights) conserves resources but risks losing morphologically complex or rare events that only appear once or twice per stay. This lever directly affects the robustness of the phenotyping dataset and the credibility of inter-rater scoring for Aim 2.
options: Escalate to full PSG on every technician-flagged event regardless of signal clarity, ensuring comprehensive capture at the cost of equipment wear and scheduling contention when multiple participants flag on the same night.

Establish a triage score combining technician confidence, sensor concordance, and participant sleep stage markers, escalating only events exceeding a pre-registered threshold and reviewing under-threshold events offline for missed captures.

Implement escalation only for the first two flagged events per participant and for any event differing morphologically from prior captures, reserving full PSG for clustering patterns and new phenomenology.
levers.review_lever: Conservative escalation preserves budget and equipment but risks systematic bias toward frequent, stereotyped events and miss of rare variant presentations; no option addresses the feedback loop where escalation history influences technician flagging behavior and confidence.

levers.name: Dual Scoring Variability and Algorithm Training Target
levers.consequences: Recruiting independent raters from the University of Bonn's sleep medicine community versus bringing in external neurophysiology specialists determines both inter-rater reliability ceiling and the training data quality for the semi-automated event-triage tools. Internal raters (lower travel cost, local AASM familiarity) may carry correlated biases from shared training; external raters (higher cost, diverse backgrounds) introduce heterogeneity in scoring style that benchmarks robustness but complicates algorithm training. The divergence between raters directly shapes reported sensitivity and specificity of Aim 3's triage model and the generalizability of published scoring rules.
options: Engage two sleep medicine faculty at University of Bonn and a third remote specialist from a different German sleep center, balancing cost and geographic diversity while maintaining AASM-standard training.

Recruit both raters from outside Bonn—a European sleep neurophysiology center and a North American group—ensuring independence and heterogeneous scoring baselines despite doubling travel and coordination overhead.

Employ one senior Bonn-based sleep specialist and train one postdoctoral researcher to criterion-level agreement, reducing external costs and creating long-term institutional capacity at the risk of lower inter-rater diversity.
levers.review_lever: External raters validate generalizability but heterogeneous scoring styles complicate algorithm training; internal raters simplify operations but may bias the triage tool toward local idiosyncrasies if the second rater is also trained in-house.

levers.name: Control Cohort Recruitment Pressure and Benchmarking Scope
levers.consequences: Defining the target size and screening stringency for the matched-control arm shapes the reference baseline against which sensor false positives and algorithm performance are evaluated. Recruiting a large, rigorously screened control cohort (stratified by age, sex, BMI, sleep stage distribution) provides robust benchmarking but delays publication and diverts recruitment resources from the higher-yield parasomnia participants; a smaller, convenience-based control group (e.g., staff self-volunteering) accelerates algorithm validation but leaves unaddressed confounding from demographics and sleep architecture. This choice influences whether the triage tool's reported specificity reflects true generalization or artifact of the control population's similarity to parasomnia participants.
options: Enroll a matched control group of 15–20 participants stratified to age, sex, and BMI ranges from the parasomnia cohort, with identical 2- to 8-week residential stays to capture seasonal and sleep-stage variation in false positives.

Recruit 8–10 convenience controls from hospital staff and sleep clinic volunteers, run them for single overnight stays with full PSG plus continuous sensor monitoring, and use this snapshot baseline for immediate algorithm training.

Defer formal control enrollment until Aim 1 and 2 publications are submitted; use the first 10–15 parasomnia participants' baseline nights (before any events occur) as provisional controls for pilot triage development.
levers.review_lever: Convenience controls accelerate algorithm deployment but introduce systematic differences in age, sleep quality, and arousal patterns that inflate reported specificity; no option directly addresses whether controls should resemble the target clinical population or represent truly healthy sleep.

levers.name: Publication Sequence and Funding Renewal Pressure
levers.consequences: Choosing the order and timing of manuscript submissions—whether to lead with methods/operations validation (slow, credible, manuscript-heavy but low novelty), longitudinal phenotyping findings (higher impact, requires sufficient event capture and follow-up), or algorithm performance (fast, publishable earlier but builds on incomplete scoring datasets)—determines both near-term visibility for grant renewal and the credibility of downstream claims. Publishing methods-first establishes rigor but delays competitive impact; publishing phenotyping early showcases scientific findings but risks incomplete participant follow-up and scoring reliability issues; leading with algorithm papers (often co-authored with industry partners) trades methodological transparency for rapid dissemination and potential pharma partnership activation.
options: Publish a comprehensive methods paper covering facility design, participant safety outcomes, sensor synchronization, and technical validation by month 18, establishing credibility before phenotyping or algorithm papers appear.

Target a high-impact sleep or neurology journal with a longitudinal case-series or cohort characterization manuscript by month 20, combining early parasomnia event captures with preliminary phenotyping to secure visibility and leverage for Phase-Two funding.

Coordinate algorithm and methods papers simultaneously for month 22 submission, presenting triage sensitivity/specificity alongside dual-rater agreement, prioritizing novelty and algorithmic contribution over methodological depth.
levers.review_lever: Methods-first publishing establishes trust but yields lower immediate impact and may signal slow progress to funders; phenotyping-first risks incomplete data quality if participant follow-up is still ongoing during writing, while algorithm-first optimizes novelty at the cost of insufficient context on data quality and human-scoring variability.

levers.name: Data-Retention and Repository Deposition Timeline
levers.consequences: Deciding when and how to deposit the de-identified physiological dataset into a public repository (immediately after initial publication, after Aim 2 is complete, only when all papers are published) determines both the competitive window for the Bonn team's follow-on analyses and the broader scientific utility of the resource. Rapid deposition (within 6 months of first publication) maximizes research impact and funder goodwill but forfeits analysis priority and risks being scooped by groups with faster turnaround. Deferred deposition (end of grant cycle, >3 years) protects the team's publication pipeline but reduces the dataset's visibility and may violate funder expectations for open science timelines. Bedroom video is permanently excluded, but physiological/sensor data (EEG, actigraphy, EMG, respiratory, environment) is legally and ethically shareable under a data use agreement.
options: Deposit de-identified physiological and sensor data to an established sleep or neurophysiology repository (e.g., OpenNeuro, the German Sleep Consortium archive) within 6 months of the first publication, with a waiver of embargo restrictions.

Commit to deposition upon completion of Aim 2 analyses and the dual-rater scoring of all captured events, estimated at month 28–30, allowing the Bonn team 12–18 months of priority-access analysis before public release.

Reserve deposition for the final grant report at month 36, after all three primary aims are published or accepted, ensuring the team's research agenda is protected but pushing public access to end-of-project timelines.
levers.review_lever: Rapid deposition accelerates scientific impact but surrenders the team's competitive advantage in secondary analyses; late deposition protects publication priority but may not align with funder transparency mandates or the Phase-Two funding timeline.

levers.name: Stay Duration Architecture
levers.consequences: Lengthening individual participant stays (up to 10 weeks) increases event capture probability and longitudinal within-person pattern characterization, but creates booking bottlenecks that reduce total participant throughput and forces extended commitment-to-screening ratios that may suppress recruitment from those with limited leave availability. Conversely, capping stays at 2–3 weeks maximizes annual enrollment but risks substantial zero-event admissions, wasting facility capacity and staff time on unproductive residents.
options: Implement a staggered follow-up model where participants complete a 3-week baseline admission, return home for 4–6 weeks, and then participate in a second 2-week visit focused on targeted nights if their baseline capture rate fell below protocol thresholds, distributing the residential burden across two shorter episodes rather than one long stay.

Adopt a rolling 2-week fixed stay for all participants with no extension option, accepting higher rates of zero-event admissions in exchange for maximized annual throughput and predictable facility turnover, then post-hoc stratify results by whether events were captured versus not.

Establish a two-tier enrollment pathway: fast-track high-frequency parasomnia participants (self-reported 4+ episodes per month) into standard 3-week stays, and offer a separate 6–8 week extended-stay track for lower-frequency cases, explicitly accepting that the extended cohort will enroll more slowly but generate richer within-person phenotyping data for a subset.
levers.review: Longer stays reduce recruitment flexibility and burden families, while shorter stays risk wasting facility utilization on non-productive admissions; the three options do not address the clinical-vs-research tension of whether 10-week stays remain ethically proportionate to the parasomnia event frequency baseline used for inclusion.

levers.name: Technician Annotation Authority
levers.consequences: Granting night technicians real-time decision authority over which nights receive escalated full-PSG montage (based on flagged suspicious events) accelerates responsive event capture and reduces false-negative misses, but introduces inter-technician variability in flagging sensitivity and specificity, potentially creating systematic bias in which events enter the dataset. Conversely, pre-scheduling all enhanced nights (night 1, mid-stay, final night) eliminates technician bias but sacrifices responsive escalation and may miss recurrence opportunities that cluster outside those fixed windows.
options: Empower night technicians to escalate to full PSG within 2 hours of flagging a suspected parasomnia event during low-burden monitoring nights, using a simple decision tree (movement amplitude exceeding threshold AND vocalization present OR bed exit attempted), with weekly review audits and monthly retraining to track technician drift.

Pre-schedule all enhanced-PSG nights as fixed calendar dates (arrival night, nights 7–8 mid-stay, final night) for every participant, supplemented by an optional technician-triggered escalation protocol only if three suspicious events are flagged within a single 24-hour window, constraining technician discretion.

Implement a hybrid model where technicians flag suspicious events in real time but must obtain same-night or next-morning approval from the on-call senior researcher (PI or postdoctoral researcher) before escalating to full PSG, adding a gate that prevents novice technician over-escalation while preserving responsiveness and limiting overnight bottlenecks.
levers.review: Technician discretion increases event capture but introduces bias; pre-scheduling ensures consistency but sacrifices responsiveness; none of the options explicitly addresses how technician fatigue or participant-technician familiarity drift might influence flagging behavior over a 10-week admission.

levers.name: Sensor Tier Harmonization
levers.consequences: The three-tier sensor model (low-burden, enhanced-PSG, escalation) generates vast heterogeneous data streams that require asynchronous alignment and motion-artifact filtering tailored to each tier's sensor suite, slowing post-hoc curation and complicating event-triage model training on mixed-quality input. Standardizing to a single high-resolution sensor suite every night eliminates alignment overhead and improves algorithm robustness, but triples electricity costs, generates overwhelming raw data volume, occupies technician time with streaming monitoring of 8 suites simultaneously, and risks participant discomfort from excessive electrode density that suppresses naturalistic behavior.
options: Maintain the tiered model but impose strict BIDS-compatible data structure requirements at acquisition time, including automated clock synchronization via NTP, parallel motion-artifact flags from each sensor tier, and segregated annotation workflows that train the event-triage algorithm on enhanced-PSG nights only, treating low-burden nights as validation-only.

Switch to full-resolution PSG montage every night for all participants, accepting the operational burden of real-time technician monitoring and the participant discomfort trade-off, but purchasing commercial software that auto-scores standard EEG features (sleep stage, arousal count) in real time, reducing post-hoc annotation bottleneck.

Deploy a hybrid where nights 1–3 and final night use full PSG, and intervening nights use low-burden sensors plus triggered escalation, but introduce a mid-stay recalibration where participants rate comfort and sleep quality every 3 days and the clinical team may reduce electrode density for high-discomfort cases, preserving the tiered approach while flagging where the protocol might suppress naturalistic behavior.
levers.review: The tiered model reduces participant burden but complicates data curation; full resolution every night solves curation but adds operational overhead and discomfort that may suppress the very behaviors the study aims to capture, and none of the options addresses how electrode density correlates with parasomnia event likelihood.

levers.name: Control Cohort Recruitment Timing
levers.consequences: Recruiting matched controls concurrently with parasomnia participants ensures contemporaneous sensor calibration and staffing efficiency but delays publication of participant-only phenotyping findings and requires pre-committing resources to two recruitment channels simultaneously, splitting technician and coordinator effort. Recruiting controls after the parasomnia cohort is enrolled reduces initial recruitment pressure and allows the team to optimize protocols based on early participant experience, but creates a temporal gap that introduces sensor drift, protocol modifications, and staffing turnover that makes meaningful matching less tenable and delays comparative benchmarking of the event-triage algorithm.
options: Enroll matched controls concurrently, targeting 1 control admission for every 1.5 parasomnia participants, with control recruitment routed through the same primary-care and neurologist networks using identical screening procedures but an exclusion criterion of any self-reported nocturnal movement or awakening, ensuring tight temporal matching and uniform sensor configuration.

Delay control enrollment until parasomnia recruitment reaches 35 participants at approximately month 18, then conduct controls over months 18–30 using identical protocols and sensor suites as they exist at that timepoint, accepting a 6-month offset in exchange for operational simplicity and allowing early publications on parasomnia phenotyping alone.

Implement a rolling control cohort where control admissions occur in alternating months with parasomnia admissions (e.g., months 1–2 parasomnia, month 3 control, months 4–5 parasomnia, month 6 control), balancing temporal matching against recruitment cadence and enabling algorithm benchmarking as data accumulates rather than all at study endpoint.
levers.review: Concurrent controls ensure matching fidelity but dilute early recruitment effort; delayed controls simplify operations but weaken temporal alignment and defer algorithm benchmarking; none directly addresses whether the control population's absence of any nocturnal movement is itself clinically unrealistic or creates a non-comparable reference baseline.

levers.name: Inter-Rater Scoring Workflow
levers.consequences: Requiring two independent raters to score all captured events (per AASM criteria) establishes ground truth reliability but demands substantial time commitment from sleep medicine experts, creating a bottleneck where scoring lags data acquisition and limits the number of events the team can process within budget. Implementing single-rater scoring with algorithmic pre-triage reduces expert time but sacrifices reliability transparency and introduces single-scorer bias that the event-triage algorithm will learn to replicate. A hybrid approach (single rater for low-confidence events flagged by the algorithm, dual raters only for borderline or discordant cases) balances efficiency and quality but risks systematic undercounting of algorithm-excluded events.
options: Maintain dual-rater scoring for all captured events, with disagreement arbitration via consensus meeting chaired by the PI, and explicitly budget 0.5 FTE sleep medicine specialist time for year 2–3, accepting that scoring will lag data acquisition by 2–4 weeks and may constrain the final event count relative to raw captures.

Deploy a single-rater scoring model where the lead postdoctoral researcher or sleep medicine specialist scores all enhanced-PSG nights and escalation events, with a sub-sample of 20% of scored nights re-scored independently by a second rater to estimate inter-rater reliability retrospectively and report the uncertainty bound in publications.

Implement a three-tier scoring cascade: the algorithm provides confidence scores for suspected parasomnia events; high-confidence events (top 10% of algorithm output) undergo single-rater scoring; medium-confidence events undergo dual-rater scoring with consensus arbitration; low-confidence events are flagged for discussion but may be excluded from primary analysis if both raters assign low clinical probability.
levers.review: Dual-rater scoring guarantees reliability but creates a labor bottleneck; single-rater reduces burden but sacrifices objectivity; three-tier triage may bias the final event sample toward high-confidence cases that are less representative of the full parasomnia spectrum.

levers.name: Facility Expansion Trigger Logic
levers.consequences: The plan defers expansion to 12 suites until pilot data demonstrate acceptable quality and safety; this staged approach controls financial risk and allows protocol refinement on a smaller footprint, but foregoes economies of scale in staff deployment, facility overhead, and sensor procurement spread over 8 versus 12 units. Conversely, committing to full 12-suite build-out at launch maximizes long-term cost efficiency and demonstrates early ambition to funders and recruiting clinicians, but locks substantial capital into infrastructure before validating demand, data quality, and the unit's ability to safely manage higher patient density and staffing complexity.
options: Remain at 8 suites throughout the 3-year period with no expansion, focusing resources on protocol validation and publication output, then propose a follow-up phase-two grant for expansion and intervention studies based on the de-identified dataset and proof-of-concept results, positioning the original unit as a methodologically validated pilot.

Build out the full 12 suites during year-one renovation but operate them in phased activation: suites 1–8 launch in month 3, suites 9–10 activate in month 12 after pilot data review, and suites 11–12 activate in month 18 only if enrollment and event-capture rates exceed thresholds, using contingent capital deployment to control risk while preserving expansion flexibility.

Execute a mid-study expansion decision point at month 18 where enrollment, safety, and staffing data determine whether to build out the remaining 4 suites; if thresholds are met (25+ enrolled, zero serious adverse events, technician retention >80%), renovation and equipping occurs in months 18–20 with expanded operations in months 21–36, accepting the risk that late expansion compresses the operational window.
levers.review: Staged expansion reduces upfront capital risk but forgoes efficiency gains; full build-out maximizes long-term cost per participant but risks underutilization; none of the options explicitly addresses whether facility reputation and clinician referral patterns depend on visible capacity or enrollment velocity.

levers.name: Pharmaceutical Partnership Governance
levers.consequences: Forgoing industry partnership retains full operational independence and publication autonomy but eliminates potential supplemental funding and industry-driven early validation interest, forcing reliance on academic grants and placing the unit at risk if DFG renewal is delayed or unsuccessful. A formal partnership providing upside funding accelerates resource availability and creates externally-validated endpoints, but introduces competing priorities around proprietary data, reporting timelines, and scope creep toward drug-responsive phenotypes that may distract from the primary methods-validation and longitudinal characterization aims.
options: Maintain the planned independent academic structure with no pharmaceutical partnership, reserving partnership discussions for a phase-two proposal only after the core phenotyping dataset is complete and de-identified publications establish methodological credibility, signaling to potential partners that collaboration occurs from a position of proven capability.

Engage a pharmaceutical partner as a non-voting scientific collaborator with a formal data-use agreement: the partner receives quarterly updates, a 30-day pre-publication comment window, and access to de-identified datasets after study completion, but contributes supplemental funding (e.g., €400K) that covers enhanced escalation-night capacity without dictating analysis strategy.

Establish a limited-scope partnership where the industry partner funds a single sub-study within the protocol (e.g., dedicated neuropsychological phenotyping in REM sleep behavior disorder participants) rather than whole-unit support, maintaining operational independence for the core NREM parasomnia aims while generating co-authored publications on the partner-funded sub-aim.
levers.review: Independence sacrifices resource upside; full partnership risks mission creep; the three options do not clarify under what conditions academic publication velocity or clinical relevance thresholds would trigger proactive partnership outreach.

levers.name: Safety Envelope versus Behavioral Authenticity
levers.consequences: Stricter safety protocols (e.g., continuous staff presence, wrist actigraphy during sleep, restricted window hardware) reduce injury risk but create a more clinical atmosphere that suppresses naturalistic parasomnia expression, potentially lowering event-capture rates. Conversely, relaxed safety boundaries preserve ecological validity but increase staffing complexity and liability exposure during nocturnal episodes.
options: Enforce continuous staff presence in the residential unit during all sleep hours, with a dedicated safety monitor stationed in a central observation room equipped with live audio and motion alerts from all suites.

Implement a hybrid model: unrestricted movement with passive environmental sensors (door alarms, bed pressure pads, infrared motion detection) triggering automated staff alerts only when thresholds suggest injury risk or egress patterns.

Adopt a risk-stratified approach where participants with documented prior injuries or high-frequency episodes receive continuous presence while lower-risk individuals operate under passive monitoring, reducing fixed staffing burden.
levers.review: Continuous presence guarantees rapid response but may inflate clinical atmosphere and suppress naturalistic behavior; relaxed monitoring captures authentic events but concentrates staffing demands unpredictably. The three options do not address whether passive-sensor false-alarm rates will overwhelm staff response capacity during multi-suite events.

levers.name: Annotation Workflow Parallelization
levers.consequences: Current protocol requires two independent raters to score all nights post-hoc against AASM criteria, creating a sequential bottleneck—if average stay is 4 weeks at 8 active suites, that is roughly 2,240 nights per year requiring dual scoring. Introducing real-time technician flagging reduces post-hoc review scope but risks inconsistent criteria application and potential bias. Conversely, strict post-hoc dual-rater-only scoring ensures rigor but may delay publication timelines and require hiring additional scoring personnel.
options: Establish a quality-assurance tier where the night technician applies a simplified event-triage checklist in real time (movement + arousal + duration thresholds) and flags only high-confidence candidate episodes for subsequent dual-rater scoring, reducing post-hoc review by approximately 40 percent.

Hire a dedicated full-time scoring coordinator who applies a preliminary AASM-aligned classification immediately after each night, then both raters review only coordinator-flagged events and a random 20 percent of negative nights to check false-negatives, creating a three-stage funnel.

Maintain strict post-hoc dual-rater review of all nights without technician input, ensuring methodological purity but requiring contracted external scorers to absorb the 2,000-plus annual night load without delaying analysis.
levers.review: Introducing technician flagging accelerates throughput but risks criterion drift and inter-rater disagreement on what constitutes a true parasomnia versus normal nocturnal movement. None of the options directly address how to validate that post-hoc scorers agree on technician-selected events versus rejected ones.

levers.name: Inclusion Threshold and Event-Yield Risk
levers.consequences: The current inclusion criterion (≥2 self-reported episodes per month) balances recruitment feasibility against event-capture probability, but recall bias and seasonal clustering mean some enrolled participants may generate zero captured events. Tightening inclusion criteria (e.g., ≥4 episodes/month or recent polysomnographic documentation of multiple events) increases per-participant yield but shrinks the eligible population and extends recruitment timelines. Loosening criteria (e.g., single prior episode confirmed by witness) expands the pool but dilutes event-capture rates and inflates the 20 percent unproductive-admission ceiling.
options: Adopt a two-tier enrollment pathway: prioritize participants with ≥4 self-reported episodes per month and at least one prior polysomnographic capture, while accepting participants with 2–3 episodes per month only after the pilot cohort (n=15–20) demonstrates acceptable event-yield rates, deferring recruitment burden.

Require all screened participants to complete a 2-week outpatient actigraphy-plus-sleep-diary run before residential admission to generate objective movement data that predicts residential capture yield, using actigraphy episode frequency as a continuous covariate in enrollment decisions.

Accept all screened participants meeting the 2-episodes-per-month criterion without actigraphy prequalification, but implement a staged stay protocol where participants with zero events in the first 2 weeks are offered discharge and rescheduling 3 months later if they wish, rather than extension to 10 weeks.
levers.review: Stricter inclusion reduces recruitment pool size and delays startup; looser inclusion inflates non-productive admissions and facility occupancy volatility. The options do not resolve whether to accept borderline-inclusion participants (e.g., single-episode polysomnographic captures) when recruitment falls behind schedule.

levers.name: Capital Expansion Trigger and Facility Saturation
levers.consequences: Deferring expansion to 12 suites until month 24 (per plan) minimizes financial risk if pilot data quality proves poor, but if operational validation succeeds early (by month 12), the unit reaches 8-suite saturation and begins turning away eligible participants. Expanding to 12 suites by month 15 accelerates participant throughput and captures more events, but commits capital before full operational proof and may create idle suites if staffing or recruitment falters. Conversely, committing to 12-suite build-out from the start reduces phased costs but locks in upfront capital and facility overhead.
options: Delay 12-suite expansion until month 24 while piloting a temporary overflow protocol: when 8 suites are full, enroll participants into a sister facility at University Hospital Bonn's clinical sleep lab on a time-shared basis (same protocols, staff, scoring pipeline), de-risking capacity bottlenecks without permanent footprint expansion.

Trigger expansion to 10 suites (rather than 12) at month 15 if: enrollment rate ≥4 participants per month and event-capture rate ≥90 percent of plan assumptions, phasing the infrastructure and hiring incrementally to match observed demand.

Commit to full 12-suite renovation and staffing by month 12, accepting upfront financial risk in exchange for eliminating capacity constraints and demonstrating scale to DFG funders before the year-two operational phase.
levers.review: Early expansion captures more data and demonstrates scale but risks underutilization if recruitment or event-yield falters; delayed expansion protects capital but may saturate the unit and create a bottleneck. None of the options address what to do if operational costs per participant prove higher than budgeted, reducing the marginal return of extra suites.

levers.name: Matched Control Enrollment Synchrony
levers.consequences: Enrolling matched controls concurrently with case participants (as assumed in current planning) ensures temporal alignment for sensor-algorithm benchmarking but increases per-night costs and staffing overhead proportionally—if cases occupy 4 suites and controls occupy 2 suites simultaneously, facility utilization is higher but fixed costs per case-event increase. Deferring control enrollment until after case phenotyping is complete reduces near-term staffing load and allows focusing recruitment on high-yield cases first, but delays the event-triage algorithm training and introduces temporal differences (e.g., seasonal sensor drift, software versioning) that complicate comparison.
options: Maintain parallel enrollment of cases and matched controls from month 6 onward, aiming for a 4:1 case-to-control ratio (40 cases, 10 controls) to balance benchmarking requirements against facility efficiency, accepting elevated overnight staffing costs for two additional suites.

Enroll all 50–70 case participants in the first 18 months, then dedicate months 19–30 to recruiting and retaining 15–20 matched controls under identical protocols, allowing control-group analysis to serve as a validation cohort for algorithm development without competing for recruitment resources.

Use a rolling cohort model: recruit controls in matched pairs immediately after every fifth case admission, distributing control enrollment evenly across the 3-year period and allowing incremental algorithmic validation as the case phenotyping dataset matures.
levers.review: Concurrent controls maximize internal validity but inflate operational complexity; sequential controls reduce near-term burden but risk temporal confounds and delay algorithm benchmarking by 18 months. The options do not specify how to handle unmatched controls if case recruitment falls short of the 50–70 target.

levers.name: External Advisory Board Authority and Budget Gates
levers.consequences: Granting the scientific advisory board approval rights for budget reallocations above €50K (per plan) provides fiscal oversight and expert scrutiny but may slow operational decisions during urgent needs (e.g., emergency equipment repair, rapid staff hiring to cover absences). Conversely, concentrating reallocation authority entirely in the PI accelerates responsive decisions but increases risk of off-plan spending and reduces external accountability. A middle ground—allowing the PI to approve reallocations up to a threshold and requiring board sign-off for larger moves—balances agility and governance.
options: Establish a tiered approval matrix: PI authority for reallocations ≤€30K with board post-hoc review at quarterly meetings; €30–75K reallocations require asynchronous board consultation within 2 weeks; reallocations >€75K require board convening within 14 days, with emergency exceptions (safety incidents, compliance violations) allowing PI discretion if board is notified within 48 hours.

Maintain strict €50K threshold with mandatory board approval, but implement a 'presumptive approval' rule where if the board does not object in writing within 10 business days of a reallocation request, the PI proceeds automatically, reducing decision latency for non-controversial moves.

Reduce board oversight to strategic milestones (Aim-completion approval, publication sign-off, year-two funding allocation) while delegating all quarterly operational budget reallocations to the PI and study coordinator, requiring only annual reconciliation reports to the board.
levers.review: Strict board gatekeeping ensures accountability but may paralyze operational agility; PI autonomy risks fiscal drift and reduces external oversight. The options do not address how to resolve conflicts if the board and PI disagree on a reallocation's scientific merit versus cost necessity.

levers.name: Data-Sharing Timeline and Publication Sequencing
levers.consequences: Publishing phenotyping and methods results before depositing the de-identified physiological dataset in a public repository (a typical 12–18 month lag) maximizes competitive advantage and allows the core team to produce secondary analyses first. However, it delays community access to the resource and risks external researchers conducting analyses in parallel. Accelerating data release (e.g., concurrent with first publication or within 6 months of close-out) fosters open science and enables rapid community validation but surrenders first-mover advantage on clinical insights and algorithmic applications.
options: Deposit de-identified physiological and sensor data in a recognized public repository (e.g., OpenNeuro) within 6 months of study close-out (month 36), contingent on publication of at least one major phenotyping manuscript, allowing the core team priority time for primary analyses while committing to timely release.

Release data immediately upon publication of the primary results manuscript (Aim 2 characterization), without awaiting completion of the event-triage algorithm, permitting external researchers to develop competing or complementary segmentation tools while core-team algorithm development continues in parallel.

Establish a managed-access data-sharing model: deposit data in a controlled repository with access granted only to researchers whose analysis plans are pre-approved by the advisory board and PI, maintaining quality control and preventing redundant or low-rigor secondary analyses.
levers.review: Early release accelerates community science but cedes competitive advantage and publication priority; delayed release protects IP but risks obsolescence and external pressure. The options do not directly address whether de-identified video data (if later released) would require additional governance or whether commercial reuse of physiological data should be permitted.

levers.name: Naturalism Calibration and Detection Trade-off
levers.consequences: Choosing how visible and intrusive the monitoring ecosystem is fundamentally affects whether participants exhibit authentic parasomnias or suppress behaviors under observation. Highly visible cameras, prominent electrode setups, and obvious safety modifications reduce ecological validity but improve event capture certainty; conversely, minimizing environmental cues and relegating sensors to dry electrodes and ambient arrays preserves behavior fidelity but increases false-positive burden on annotation and triage algorithms. This balance directly shapes the utility of captured events for phenotyping and the credibility of absence-of-events claims in control participants.
options: Deploy cameras in corners with warm ambient lighting and introduce them during a one-week acclimatization period before formal monitoring, treating the environment as a familiar bedroom rather than a clinical lab space.

Equip suites with clinical-grade visible electrode montages and safety railings throughout, accepting a higher proportion of suppressed events in exchange for unambiguous physiological signal quality and uncontested safety documentation.

Rely primarily on hidden mattress and bed-frame sensors with minimal visible apparatus, using infrared cameras only when technician-flagged events occur, preserving naturalism at the cost of delayed full-resolution capture on first occurrence.
levers.review: Invisible sensor arrays preserve behavior authenticity but shift the annotation bottleneck to real-time technician judgment about which partial-signal events warrant escalation; no option resolves the fundamental tension between ecological validity and detection completeness during the baseline-monitoring nights.

levers.name: Roster Flexibility and Night-Shift Continuity
levers.consequences: Staffing night coverage with a fixed 3-technician rotating roster ensures predictable labor costs and team cohesion but locks the unit into a staffing model sized to 8 active suites with minimal slack for illness, vacation, or unexpected surge in event-flagging workload. Alternatively, building a larger flexible pool with on-call backup increases payroll and coordination overhead but absorbs staffing shocks and allows expansion trials without rehiring. The choice cascades into whether the unit can safely and ethically extend stays for zero-yield participants or must discharge them promptly to preserve technician capacity.
options: Maintain a dedicated 3-person night team on rotating 12-hour shifts with strict leave-replacement budgeting, accepting a hard operational ceiling of 7 concurrent participants before staffing becomes unsafe.

Recruit a 4- to 5-person core team plus 1–2 part-time per-diem technicians on-call, absorbing higher baseline payroll to enable flexible capacity scaling and event-driven escalation nights without burnout risk.

Cross-train the day-shift clinical psychologist and data engineer as backup technicians for light-monitoring nights, minimizing new hires and reserving the core night team for high-event-yield periods and complex annotation decisions.
levers.review: Flexible rosters address staffing volatility but blur role clarity and introduce training variance if part-time staff rotate infrequently; none of the three options structurally solve the annotation bottleneck if event frequency exceeds technician throughput.

levers.name: Escalation Night Trigger and Triage Burden
levers.consequences: Defining the threshold at which a technician-flagged partial-signal event prompts deployment of full PSG montage on an escalation night determines both the sensitivity of the capture model and the operational cost per event. Aggressive escalation (low threshold, many escalation nights per participant) guarantees clinical-grade recapture but taxes equipment, staffing, and the budget; conservative escalation (high threshold, fewer escalation nights) conserves resources but risks losing morphologically complex or rare events that only appear once or twice per stay. This lever directly affects the robustness of the phenotyping dataset and the credibility of inter-rater scoring for Aim 2.
options: Escalate to full PSG on every technician-flagged event regardless of signal clarity, ensuring comprehensive capture at the cost of equipment wear and scheduling contention when multiple participants flag on the same night.

Establish a triage score combining technician confidence, sensor concordance, and participant sleep stage markers, escalating only events exceeding a pre-registered threshold and reviewing under-threshold events offline for missed captures.

Implement escalation only for the first two flagged events per participant and for any event differing morphologically from prior captures, reserving full PSG for clustering patterns and new phenomenology.
levers.review: Conservative escalation preserves budget and equipment but risks systematic bias toward frequent, stereotyped events and miss of rare variant presentations; no option addresses the feedback loop where escalation history influences technician flagging behavior and confidence.

levers.name: Dual Scoring Variability and Algorithm Training Target
levers.consequences: Recruiting independent raters from the University of Bonn's sleep medicine community versus bringing in external neurophysiology specialists determines both inter-rater reliability ceiling and the training data quality for the semi-automated event-triage tools. Internal raters (lower travel cost, local AASM familiarity) may carry correlated biases from shared training; external raters (higher cost, diverse backgrounds) introduce heterogeneity in scoring style that benchmarks robustness but complicates algorithm training. The divergence between raters directly shapes reported sensitivity and specificity of Aim 3's triage model and the generalizability of published scoring rules.
options: Engage two sleep medicine faculty at University of Bonn and a third remote specialist from a different German sleep center, balancing cost and geographic diversity while maintaining AASM-standard training.

Recruit both raters from outside Bonn—a European sleep neurophysiology center and a North American group—ensuring independence and heterogeneous scoring baselines despite doubling travel and coordination overhead.

Employ one senior Bonn-based sleep specialist and train one postdoctoral researcher to criterion-level agreement, reducing external costs and creating long-term institutional capacity at the risk of lower inter-rater diversity.
levers.review: External raters validate generalizability but heterogeneous scoring styles complicate algorithm training; internal raters simplify operations but may bias the triage tool toward local idiosyncrasies if the second rater is also trained in-house.

levers.name: Control Cohort Recruitment Pressure and Benchmarking Scope
levers.consequences: Defining the target size and screening stringency for the matched-control arm shapes the reference baseline against which sensor false positives and algorithm performance are evaluated. Recruiting a large, rigorously screened control cohort (stratified by age, sex, BMI, sleep stage distribution) provides robust benchmarking but delays publication and diverts recruitment resources from the higher-yield parasomnia participants; a smaller, convenience-based control group (e.g., staff self-volunteering) accelerates algorithm validation but leaves unaddressed confounding from demographics and sleep architecture. This choice influences whether the triage tool's reported specificity reflects true generalization or artifact of the control population's similarity to parasomnia participants.
options: Enroll a matched control group of 15–20 participants stratified to age, sex, and BMI ranges from the parasomnia cohort, with identical 2- to 8-week residential stays to capture seasonal and sleep-stage variation in false positives.

Recruit 8–10 convenience controls from hospital staff and sleep clinic volunteers, run them for single overnight stays with full PSG plus continuous sensor monitoring, and use this snapshot baseline for immediate algorithm training.
